title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation
authors: Jielun Chen, Jiace Sun, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan
abstract: The first-principles quantum simulation of the full electronic Hamiltonian of a material model of realistic size appears daunting even in a future era of fully fault-tolerant quantum computers. In contrast, classical simulations of material excited states rely on heuristic quasiparticle frameworks, such as the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation, where only a few quasiparticles are explicitly considered. Here we give a detailed description of quasiparticle quantum simulation for multi-excitonic states within the BSE. We develop an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, and reduce its cost using integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For a materials model of size $N$, and a fixed number of quasiparticles, the resulting algorithms require $\widetilde{O}(N)$ Toffoli gates and $O(\log N)$ logical qubits, or, using space-time tradeoffs, $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ Toffoli gates and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ logical qubits, achieving up to a sixth power reduction in Toffoli count, or up to exponential reduction in qubit count, versus standard full Hamiltonian simulation techniques that have been explored in materials simulation. Resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation across a range of semiconductor models of a realistic physical size of $O(10^3)$ atoms, show that our Toffoli-optimized implementation reduces the Toffoli count by $10^6-10^7$ relative to full Hamiltonian simulation estimates, while a qubit-optimized implementation requires only a few hundred logical qubits. More broadly, these results show that classical heuristic frameworks will be essential in the design of future fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for materials.
summary: This paper details a method for quantum simulation of multi-excitonic states using the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) within a quasiparticle framework. By encoding the BSE Hamiltonian into a qubit circuit, the authors demonstrate significant resource savings—up to an exponential reduction in qubits—compared to simulating the full electronic Hamiltonian. This confirms that classical heuristic approximations are crucial for designing feasible future quantum algorithms for materials science.
main_problem: Developing resource-efficient quantum algorithms to simulate multi-excitonic states governed by the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) in materials.
main_result: The quasiparticle approach offers exponential reductions in quantum resources (Toffoli gates and qubits) compared to simulating the full electronic Hamiltonian.
method: The authors developed an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, employing integral factorization and crystal symmetries for optimization.
model_or_system: The simulation targets multi-excitonic states in materials, modeled using first-principles approaches and governed by the BSE, which is derived from the full electronic Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Excitation energies, Toffoli gate count, and logical qubit count.
important_parameters: System size N (up to $10^3$ atoms), number of quasiparticles, and k-point mesh size ($N_k$).
main_assumptions: The use of heuristic quasiparticle approximations (GW/BSE) and the assumption of exponential localization of orbitals for convergence proofs.
figures_summary: Table V provides detailed resource estimates (Toffoli counts, logical qubits) for various materials across different k-point meshes, showing scaling behavior.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the difficulty of full Hamiltonian simulation to detailing the BSE formulation, developing the qubit encoding, optimizing the resource scaling, and finally presenting resource estimates for specific materials.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the resource scaling for simulating complex many-body quantum systems (excitons) using quantum computation primitives, which is highly relevant to quantum algorithms for condensed matter physics.

Figure 3. Quantum and classical resource estimates for diamond. The BSE calculations use m = 3, a THC fitting tolerance of 0.1 mEh MP2 error per unit cell, and no space-group adaptation. All quantum methods target 0.1 eV QPE error per eigenvalue estimate: an excitation energy for BSE and a total supercell energy for the full-Hamiltonian methods. Constant overheads for combining ground- and excited-state estimates are omitted. (a) Quantum Toffoli counts and classical BSE FLOPs. (b) Logical qubits and classical BSE storage, counted in floating-point values. Open markers denote extrapolated data.

Figure 4. All cases use m = 3 unless oth- erwise labelled. (a) Toffoli counts without (blue) and with (orange) space-group adaptation.
